title: Eye contact is not the only way adults and babies stay engaged
summary: Akhtar and Gernsbacher write that some communities hold babies facing outward, so mutual gaze is less common, and touch and voice can carry the engagement.
body: A 2008 review says theories often treat mutual gaze as the sign of social engagement. Nameera Akhtar and Morton Ann Gernsbacher answer that cultures differ in how babies are held. They report observations that Kaluli mothers in Papua New Guinea hold infants facing out, and that those mothers and infants do not gaze into each other's eyes, in line with adult talk that also avoids gaze while speaking. They also report less mutual gaze when Palestinian families hold babies on the lap more than Israeli families do. Their conclusion is that a lack of eye contact does not mean a lack of engagement, because touch, posture, and voice can do that work. The comparisons are the ones this review cites, and the card does not rank cultures.

sources.title: On privileging the role of gaze in infant social cognition
sources.author: Nameera Akhtar and Morton Ann Gernsbacher
sources.note: Supports the Kaluli holding example, the Palestinian and Israeli holding contrast as the review states it, and the conclusion that missing eye contact is not missing engagement. Peer-reviewed open copy. Paraphrased.

said_by: Nameera Akhtar and Morton Ann Gernsbacher
